No. The
resolution before us is an important one. It has been commented upon in the press, and is a very far-rea-ching matter. Before we just drop it out of sight I think it would be well to have before the committee and the public some of the considerations involved in it.
I propose therefore to read a lengthy dispatch from the Winnipeg Free Press of February 21, in which this resolution is commented upon, because I take it that it was the difficulties mentioned in this extract I am about to read which caused the government to reconsider its position. I believe we would understand the situation better if the parliamentary assistant would take us just a little more into his confidence. This article in the Winnipeg Free Press, by Victor Mackie, states:
Millions of dollars of imports will be affected by the proposed amendment to the Customs Tariff involving motive power for machinery, introduced into parliament by Hon. Douglas Abbott, Minister of Finance, in his budget.
So sweeping is the wording of the proposed amendment that there are serious questions being raised here as to whether it may involve a breach of the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
The machinery item, of a class or kind not made in Canada (item 427A) is a bound item under GATT. The proposed amendment would remove from that item detachable motors, such as electric motors or other types of motive power. It would in effect make the motors dutiable at a higher rate of tariff and consequently it could be argued that it was a clear breach of GATT.
However the national revenue department presumably would reply that it was not a breach of GATT because for years it has been separating electric motors from machinery imports for the purposes of applying the tariff. There are suggestions that the amendment included in the budget will have to be reworded-
That was a bit of inspiration, apparently, on the part of the correspondent.
-and made more specific before it is presented to parliament for approval.
And later in the same article:
This wording is sweeping, taking in not only electrical motors but all other types of motive power.
There are indications that it may be redrafted and made to apply to electrical motors, particularly.

I wish to read further from this article, because evidently this has been a matter of considerable difficulty. It has been before the tariff board. I shall read further from this extract, where it deals with the discussions before that board:
If machinery of a class or kind not made in Canada is admissible for duty purposes with its electric motor as one entity the whole only pays a tariff of 71 per cent. But if the electric motor is detached and a tariff imposed against the motor separately, it pays a high tariff of 221 per cent.
The tariff board ruled on the cases that came before it that the electric motors as part of machinery were entities and it did not matter whether they were detached. The motor and machine paid the low rate. After these rulings Dave Sim, the deputy minister of national revenue, asked the tariff board for guidance as to whether it had been applying the "proper principle" in the past in ruling that the electric motor should be detached and made dutiable as a separate entity.
For years the department has sought to apply the rule that if the motor could be detached then it should be dutiable at the higher rate of duty as a separate entity.
The tariff board held hearings on the request of the deputy minister for guidance. It had not yet reached a decision when the budget was brought down incorporating the board amendment that "machinery" will not include motive power which when detached from the machine will operate. It is believed that in the light of the budget resolution the request to the board for guidance will now be withdrawn.
Parliament when it enacts the amendment as proposed in the budget, or a rewritten amendment, will establish the principle of whether electric motors are to be dutiable at a higher rate of duty when detachable.
I have brought this before the committee because it does seem to me that after a month-and it is just a month since the rapturous night of the budget; it is quieter now-we might have had from the parliamentary assistant who, I am sure, wishes to be co-operative in every possible way, something more than merely a statement that this was going to be, as I think he said, "dropped." I do not know whether he said, "dropped for rewording." The parliamentary assistant used very much the same language as the minister used the other day when talking about the excise tax, something about the difficulty of technical wording. I cannot find the exact phrase.
I raise this because it seems to me the matter has most important implications. It raises the question of our membership in the general agreement on tariffs and trade; it raises the question of the criticisms we have been making of the United States for its exclusive attitudes in the matter of tariffs; it raises the question as to the implications of the conversations which were had by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance in London in December; it raises the question which was raised vividly by the chancellor

of the British exchequer when he was here a week ago. For these reasons I thought it worth while to try to expose to the house the very important principles involved and the important economic consequences that may follow, and also the relationships which we have assumed in various ways with other countries.

Then I have been very stupid. 1 did not fully understand the parliamentary assistant when he said that it should be dropped. I was wrong in thinking there was a possibility of it coming back. Apparently it is being dropped out of sight.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Resolution No. 1 has been
dropped, so there is nothing to add. It is not half-dropped, as the Minister of National Revenue tells me.

What happens if you want to
discuss something which is not included in the printed list? The chairman has ruled already that we can discuss only things that are related to the items as printed. I should like to say something about certain accessories to hearing aids. Could that be included under machinery?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If it is relevant the hon. member can speak about it, but if it is not relevant I am afraid he cannot speak about hearing aids on the machinery item. The suggestion is made by the parliamentary assistant that we proceed by calling these tariff items one by one. Is that procedure agreed to?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 105c.

To begin with I might say I am very fond of olives, but I am curious and a little disturbed to see that they are going to be dutiable after July 1, 1954, as I read the schedule. How is the government able to look ahead for nearly eighteen months and decide that this item which is to be free up to July 1, 1954 will thereafter be faced with a tariff varying from 10 per cent to 30 per cent? I am sure those who like olives or who attend cocktail parties will share my concern.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The budget of 1952 provided for a change in the tariff on this item to be in effect for one year, up to July 1, 1953. We are proposing to provide the change for another year. Next year parliament will have an opportunity to look at the matter again. The rates of free, free and 30 per cent will be in effect until July 1, 1954, and

Customs Tariff
next year parliament will have an opportunity to look at the matter and decide what it will be after July 1, 1954.

I am grateful for that explanation by the parliamentary assistant. Is there an olive-growing industry in Canada which requires some protection? Is that why you are doing this only from year to year instead of eliminating it altogether?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.

I do not suppose the loss of revenue would be very great. Surely there has been sufficient experience gained during the year in which they have been free. There would not seem to be such a great loss of revenue that you would have to put the duty back on. Why don't you just drop it altogether?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is done at this time for the improvement of our trade with Spain, Greece and Italy, but we want to be as careful as we can so that we may keep this item for bargaining purposes.
Would Spain, Greece and Italy come under the most-favoured-nation tariff or under the general tariff?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Under the most-favourednation tariff.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We will pass on to item No. 173.

I am glad that the list of books to be admitted free to this country has been extended. The fourth part of this item reads:
Single copies of books when sent to a reviewer of books for bona fide review purposes; single copies1 of books when sent unsolicited and without charge to faculty members of universities or colleges.
There is another class of books which I suggest should also be free when imported. I refer to textbooks bought by qualified professors of universities or colleges which are outside the curriculum with which they are concerned. From the point of view of education it is essential that these professors should have this type of book. If a professor at the University of Saskatchewan, McGill or some other university decides that he should have certain background material- and in my opinion it is essential that he should have background material not definitely upon the curriculum, reference works by which he can increase his own knowledge of the subject and so become a more efficient teacher of it-then he certainly should be allowed to import such books free of duty. The fact that they are not on the free list now may be for the reason that the matter has simply been overlooked because,

as I interpret the new spirit with reference to the business of books, and particularly with respect to the abolition of the sales tax, something for which I have worked for years and upon which I congratulate the government, I should think the government would also be in favour of adding that one classification of books to the duty free list.
Any man who is going to teach a course must have a wide background of reference material with respect to his subject quite apart from the actual books which are on the course to be taught. I should like some comment on this matter. Even at this stage surely it should be possible to include that class of books.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I understand that if a
university professor imports such a book for use in a university library entry will be free. If it is for his own use-

That is not what I am asking. I am well aware that at the present time libraries can import books free, and I am well aware that any books on the regular curriculum of a university are admitted free. What I am asking is that the privilege which is extended to the university professor to receive an unsolicited book duty free should be extended to the case where he himself sends to the United States, let us say, and orders a reference book having to do with the course which he has to teach. I know the matter is somewhat academic and technical, and that is why I believe the government have overlooked it. With the new spirit of promotion of books I am quite sure that if the government had thought about the matter these would have been included in the list. Why in the world should a man be allowed to receive an unsolicited book duty free and yet have to pay duty on a reference work which he needs for background material in connection with one of his classes when he brings it in of his own volition rather than having it sent to him by somebody else? To me the thing is ridiculous.
Could he not get the book through his university library under item 173?

Quite often university libraries are small, or the university does not have too much money to expend on such -books. On the other hand, when a professor is willing to spend his own money for a reference book which will broaden his knowledge of the subject I think it is all for the good of himself, his classes and the country generally that a wide background of reference material should be available to him.
It is only a small matter. A professor might order perhaps two or three books in a

year. A bona fide professor of a university teaching a definite course in a particular subject should be allowed to import reference books on that subject duty free in order to assist him in his work, whether the books are solicited or unsolicited. Personally I do not see any reason for this particular clause. I would have thought that where a man expresses a need for such a book, orders it and pays for it would have been the first place to do away with the tariff. I welcome the one concession, but I think the other is more necessary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that his representations will be considered. However, I should point out to him that what he proposes now would give rise to many administrative difficulties. What would be the test? Would it be the professor's judgment? To what kind of professors should we extend this privilege? Would clergymen, for instance, ask for the same privilege? Would other classes of people ask for the same privilege? I am not entering into a debate with the hon. member. I am just making him aware of the administrative difficulties which will be studied in the light of his representations, which representations will also be most carefully and sympathetically examined.
I do not admit that there would be such difficulties as the parliamentary assistant has dragged out of an imaginary hat. He asks what is a professor? Is he a clergyman?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, no.

I say it is easy enough to establish the identity of a bona fide professor teaching in a bona fide university in Canada. It is easy enough for him to prove that he is teaching a certain course and that he needs the reference book to teach that subject. So far as I am concerned he should have it, and the fewer obstacles that are put in his way the better for him, for his classes and for education in the country generally. I am making a definite appeal. I hope I am making myself dear. I am asking that a bona fide professor of a bona fide university teaching a course in a particular subject should be able to send to the United States and buy himself a book or two books and not be charged duty on them.

I want to support my hon. friend, but I should like to go a step further. I cannot understand the parliamentary assistant's objection with respect to distinguishing what a university professor is, and the statement he made that you might have to iput lawyers and clergymen on the same list. As a matter of fact we have
Customs Tariff
narrowed the provision here to provide for unsolicited books to be received duty free by a professor in a bona fide university or college, but I should like to go one step further. In the interests of education and general culture in our country I say that books of this type should be admitted duty free whether they are imported by a university professor, a teacher or by someone interested in the subject who wishes to enlarge and improve his own education.
I think we make a mistake when we subject books of this description to any duty at all, because in this new country of ours we want to build up the best kind of libraries we -can; and individuals who can build up libraries of books of this description for their own education can make a worthwhile contribution to the country. Many of us know of individuals in the older parts of Canada, Ontario and Quebec, who have -built up libraries. Those of us who come from older countries know of individuals with quite extensive libraries of reference books.
While I support the plea of the hon. member for Saskatoon, I should like the consideration to extend to something more than that, to the free -entry of books of this description that would be useful to teachers, lawyers, doctors, -clergymen and others -who are promoting the general culture and general educational welfare and standards of the country. I should like to make that plea for the future in any event.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar has given as examples lawyers and clergymen. May I draw his attention to item 172 -under which the following books all come in free, whatever may be their source; books, pamphlets and reports for the promotion of religion, medicine and surgery, the fine arts, law, science, technical training and the study of languages. I do not know exactly what the hon. member for Saskatoon has in mind.
As a matter of fact the parliamentary assistant himself raised the question in reply to the hon. member for Saskatoon with respect to books imported by the clergy, lawyers and doctors.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not lawyers or doctors.
I did not know what the interpretation of this particular item was. If it is as narrow as I infer from the reply to my hon. friend, then I want to see it greatly expanded.

I would like to add- to the remarks -by my hon. friends to the left and go a little further in this matter. I feel that all books should be duty free. In the days

Customs Tariff
before we became part of this great dominion and were just Newfoundland, they all came in duty free. I do not see that you are any more educated up here than we are; there are a lot of people in Newfoundland who would like to buy books, and a few cents makes a difference. I see no very good reason which the parliamentary assistant can give why any duty should be imposed on books of any kind. Is it because you are trying to protect the bookmakers or booksellers here; or is the amount you require so great that we have to put taxation on books?
I will go along with that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, practically all technical books are free. There is a duty of 10 per cent on fiction, novels. It is a question of knowing whether that small protection should be left for our printing industry.
Mr. Nose worthy: May I put a question for information? With respect to the first item in 173, do I understand correctly that any teacher or student may import a book that is either an authorized textbook or a book of reference on a school course duty free?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is no change there, Mr. Chairman.
What is that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is no change in 173 (1).
I am asking what the situation is now. Are they free?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are free, Mr. Chairman. That is shown in black and white in the resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we pass on to 199j?
I have a second question on 173. What does the department require from an individual importer to indicate that a certain book is a prescribed book of reference in a school?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the department requires reasonable proof that it is on the curriculum.
Why are dictionaries not included?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Did the parliamentary
assistant hear the question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is the first request we have had along that line.
What?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is the first request that has ever come to the department, according to the information I have, for the freeing of dictionaries.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: May I interject that I think it would make it a lot simpler if it were understood that the changes, which are ordinarily underlined in an act, are here in fine print. In the first part, books, etc., that is what is in the tariff now. There is no change in part 1. When you come to the fine print under that item that is a change. By reading the two together you get a full idea of what the changes are and what already is in the tariff.
I think the parliamentary assistant misunderstood my question. I want to know why dictionaries were set aside as separate from all others, and what duty there is now on dictionaries.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The duty is 10 per cent, Mr. Chairman, and it is because they are printed in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 199j.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 237.

I would like to ask the minister why these cannot come in free under the general tariff. As I understand it, isotopes are produced for medicine, agriculture and industry; and it does seem to me that they should be free.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as my hon. friend knows the production of isotopes has been temporarily suspended; and that is the reason for the change.
Can the parliamentary assistant say whether the United States imposes a duty on Canadian isotopes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, not according to the information I have.

I thought the hon. gentleman was discussing 199j. I cannot understand why wire reinforced paper tape, printed or not, imported for use in the packaging of fruit, vegetables and other farm or garden produce should be taxed at 5 per cent when we seem to have a policy, and I think it is the policy adopted by the government, of letting farm machinery and supplies in free. It seems to me that this is a supply used in the fruit and vegetable industry; and if we allow farm equipment to be imported and used in other branches of agriculture, I cannot see why there should be a duty of 5 per cent under the British preferential tariff and the other rates of duty as given there, on something that is necessary for the fruit and vegetable industry. The packaging;

of imported fruits, vegetables and other garden or farm produce is certainly quite extensive today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
According to my information the use of these twist-ems is not very great.
I have seem some pictures of them, and they are mainly used to wrap vegetables in retail stores.

The people who buy fruits and vegetables have to pay for them. Look at the rates. There is a small decrease, but under the British preferential tariff the rate is 5 per cent and under the most-favourednation class it is 10 per cent and under the general tariff it is still 35 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not think it can be said that it is only a small reduction. It is from 25 per cent to 10 per cent under the mostfavoured-nation class; and those things were coming in from the United States.

Supposing fruit and vegetables come in, as they do very largely, packaged in the United States; is the package charged under the general tariff or what is the situation? Suppose, for example, that spinach comes into Canada in packages. Is the package valued separately from the contents and is a duty of 35 per cent charged on the package in which the spinach comes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is included; but may I stress the point that these twist-ems are not used extensively. They are used in retail stores to put for example around six bananas, and things of that nature.

But my hon. friend cannot go into many retail stores; otherwise he would know that these things are packaged and, I believe, packaged in the United States. If you walk into stores here you will sometimes see "Texas" on a package of washed vegetables or something of that sort.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The principal reason is to advertise Texas or some other place.
It may be advertising Texas, but I believe that some of these vegetables are packaged or crated in Texas.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Surely.

And if they are, and if the Canadian consumer is taxed on the package at the rate of 35 per cent, that increases the cost of these vegetables and the cost of living; and it seems to me that is entirely at variance with the policy of this parliament of allowing foodstuffs and farm supplies free into Canada. This is a supply. Perhaps I should say this. I have not much sympathy with the idea of washing and packaging turnips, carrots and spinach and everything that comes in. I think it increases the cost
Customs Tariff
of living. But it is done extensively now and people are buying them, and they expect it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am not sure that I understand exactly the point the hon. member wants to make. He speaks of a duty of 35 per cent on vegetables coming from the United States. There is no such duty of 35 per cent on vegetables coming from the United States. On the other hand, do I understand that the hon. member wants all vegetables to come from the United States free? Is that what he means?

I am talking about the packages in which the vegetables come. It is clearly stated here that the following shall be dutiable:
Wire reinforced paper tape, printed or not, imported for use in the packaging of fruit, vegetables and other farm or garden produce.
There is wire in all these things. I do not think they should be taxed. That is the point I am making.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I can say that it has been estimated that the Canadian consumption of these twist-ems items would not amount to more than $15,000 a year.
I do not know what the value is, but the principle is wrong.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are we through with our discussion on item 237? If so, the next is item 272b, petroleum waxes, et cetera.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 280, grease and oils.
May I ask what is the effect of this change, adding "and oils"? What oils will those be; what kind of oils?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The former item 280, subparagraph 2, provided for duty free entry from all countries of grease, rough, the refuse of animal fat, for the manufacture of soap and oils only. Item 280, subparagraph 3, provides for inedible oils without admixture, obtained from animal fat, for use in the manufacture of soap or oils. The two items are now combined in one item only in order to facilitate administration.
If I understand the matter correctly, there is no real change by that addition?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.
It is just a matter of combining the two of them into one?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is no change made except for administrative purposes.

All the oils that are mentioned here are non-edible oils, are they?

Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are not.
I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are not.
I am not sure that I understand what the parliamentary assistant means. Does he mean they are not edible oils?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are not edible oils.
Could they be refined or made into margarine or anything of that nature?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 403, wire rope or cable.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 409c, ploughs and parts thereof.
What does that mean? I should like to get an explanation of it. As I read it, it means that plough bolts are put into the other list. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.
That is quite a consolation to the farmers.
I was going to ask if this is where it was intended to include them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. We are on item 409c now.
Mr. Chairman-[DOT]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Battle River wants to say something. He has been trying to get the floor for some time.

I wanted to get a little bit of information from the parliamentary assistant in connection with the importation of small gasoline engines used for pumping water, running fanning mills, cement mixers and things of that kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Does that come under item 409c?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.
Not particularly; no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then shall we pass on to item 409e? Perhaps the hon. member can reserve his question until we reach an item to which it will be relevant. We are now on item 409e, spraying and dusting machines.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 409g, incubators for hatching eggs.
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 409q.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will ask my colleague the Minister of National Revenue to move an amendment to item 409f which is not in the list. It is proposed to amend this item to provide for hydraulic hoists for unloading vehicles for use on the farm for farm purposes only. That was the point raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
That is the point I raised with the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would ask the Minister of National Revenue to move that amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I move:
That the following item be inserted in resolution 3, of February 19, 1953:
409f-Grain crusher; grain or hay grinders; grain or hay dryers; milk coolers; steel stanchions for confining livestock either in pens or individually, including complete equipment for milking parlours; automatic stock watering bowls; barn litter carriers and track; sprinkler irrigation systems; barn hay forks, carriage, pulleys and track; hydraulic hoists for unloading vehicles; all the foregoing for use on the farm for farm purposes only; hay loaders, hay tedders, potato planters, potato diggers, fodder or feed cutters, ensilage cutters, post hole diggers, snaths, stumping machines, grain loaders or elevators with a capacity not exceeding 40 bushels per minute and all other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery, n.o.p., and complete parts of all the foregoing	Free-Free-Free.

I should like to express appreciation, to the minister and the department for the prompt manner in which they considered this point. I brought it to their attention only ten days ago. We have it on the free list today. I want to express my appreciation to the minister for his prompt action.
I wonder if the parliamentary assistant could satisfy my curiosity about item 409e by telling me what is apparatus for the destruction of predatory animals by the discharge of poisonous cartridges.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I know that it is usually called a coyote-getter.
Which item are we on, Mr. Chairman? Are we on the amendment that was moved?
That is what I was going to ask.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We were on the amendment that was offered until the hon. member for Greenwood interjected a question having to do with item 409e which was carried a few moments ago. But I presumed it was with the unanimous consent of the committee that such question was asked. We therefore come back to item 409f. That is the amendment

which was offered. Does the hon. member wish to speak to the amendment?

Yes. It was carried rather
hurriedly and some of us did not realize it. Like the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I was pleased to hear this amendment; but I was rather disappointed that grindstones for mowing machines were not included. All farmers who cut grain and hay with certain types of machinery use grindstones for mowing machines. As grinders were mentioned for other machinery used on the farm, it does not seem logical to exclude grindstones used for mowing machines or grain-cutting machines. I would urge the minister to give consideration to the inclusion of these grindstones.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that consideration will be given to his representation.

I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant what is the change in the item covering equipment for confining livestock either in pens or individually, including complete equipment for milking parlours; automatic stock-watering bowls; barn litter carriers and track; sprinkler irrigation systems, etc. Can he tell me what the change is?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is no change in the item. The only change is to add to the list "hydraulic hoists for unloading vehicles".
Otherwise it is exactly the same?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is identical.

I should like to ask a question in connection with, sprinkler irrigation systems. The parliamentary assistant may remember that two years ago I had quite a long discussion with the minister in connection with this particular matter. Do these sprinkler irrigation systems include the pumps and engines which work them? Is that now the interpretation placed on this item?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am informed that the answer is yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we now pass on to 409q?

Perhaps I can get the information I want under this item. I want to find out what the regulations are in connection with the importation of small gasoline engines to be used on pumps, fanning mills, small cement mixers and things of that kind. Do they come in free of duty?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I do not believe cement mixers could be considered as agricultural implements.
Customs Tariff
Well, call it a fanning mill or a pump engine or a small grain loader or something of that kind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, for fanning mills; any agricultural implement is free under this item.
With engines attached to them? I refer to small combustion engines up to 5 horsepower.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If they are to be attached; if incorporated, they are free.

What is the definition of "attached" and the word "auxiliary"? There must be some definition, because I was charged duty a couple of years ago on bringing in one to be attached. I should like to know what the definition of "attached" is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Was it before 1950?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There has been a change since.

Over a year and a half ago I bought an electric motor to work a pump, and I certainly had to pay duty on it. There seemed to be no relaxation of duty as far as electric motors for that purpose were concerned at that time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: A pump is not necessarily an agricultural implement. Moreover, that is one of the definitions that prompted the dropping of resolution 1.

I think that was the very point we were trying to get at, namely the definition of an agricultural implement, or what sort of motor was meant that would be attached to it. Certainly a pump on a farm used entirely for watering livestock is a piece of agricultural machinery. There is no question about that.

I want to pursue that a little farther. When I was home during the Christmas recess one of the machine agents handed me a form, in fact forms from two companies, and they read like this:
I also certify that the internal combustion engine described is being purchased by me for installation on my farm and that this engine will be used for agricultural purposes only and will be incorporated in or attached to agricultural machinery as classified by the Canadian customs act which permits an internal combustion engine to be imported free of duty and sales tax only if used to operate the following farm machinery:
Then follow a number of farm machines. In other parts of the form it states that it has to be bolted down or attached solidly on one particular piece of machinery and cannot be used around the farm. When I was farming we had part of the time one pump engine

Customs Tariff
which was from 2J to 3 horsepower. It was a gasoline engine. When the time came either in the fall or spring, whichever was convenient, to clean grain, where we had only-one gasoline engine we took it off a pump and used it on the fanning mill. According to another part of this form the dealer's certificate reads like this:
I/we certify that the above certificate is correct. I/we agree to indemnify the Canadian Fairbanks-Morse Company Limited in the event that a customs inspection should prove this sale unqualified for duty exemption.
At the bottom of the form we find the following:
Warning-An engine used for attachment to cement mixers, wood sawing machines, pump jacks, water pumps, et cetera does not qualify for duty and tax exemption as this equipment is not classified in the customs tariff as agricultural machinery.
To me that is one of the craziest things in the world, because if you do not have to use it for pumps or fanning mills on the farm you do have to use these small wood-sawing machines to saw wood. I think this item needs revision and I should like to know what comment the parliamentary assistant has in this connection.

I should like to support what the hon. member says. Surely the department should be interested in getting the most efficient operation of engines on the farm. If you are going to say that the engine must be attached to the machine, it means that if you are going to use the engine on the fanning mill you have to attach the engine to it. But you do not operate that way. You attach the fanning mill to the skids and attach the engine to the skids as well. With respect to grain loaders, today we do have engines attached to grain loaders; but there is nothing to stop a farmer taking them off and using them on other machines. Instead of the word "attached" the words used should be "used for the operation of". The great majority of engines are not attached to machines. Certainly you are going to make farming more expensive if you are going to insist that a specific farm machine must have an engine attached to it in order to benefit from this resolution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The greatest consideration will be given to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Acadia.

Some consideration should be given to having the tariff reduced here, particularly for gold mining which is in such a bad way at the present time.

These pumps are the pumps which I imagine would be operating what are known as the Oliver filters and the American filters which extract the gold from the cyanide solution which is known as the pregnant solution. They are used in the process of extracting the precious metals from this solution and are a very important item in any milling operation. It seems that these pumps, which are a very essential part of any precious metal mine, are taxed at the highest rate of any in the schedule. I wondered whether there was any reason for this, particularly as precious metal mines, both gold and silver, are in a very serious position at the present time.

I have raised the point because for some considerable "time the tariff, excise tax and sales tax on gas stoves have been very much in excess of those on coal stoves. I come from an area in which practically all cooking and heating is done by gas. I have been interested in this matter for some time, and have brought it to the attention of the Minister of Finance in previous years.
I submit that there should be no distinction between coal and gas stoves used for cooking or heating purposes. The result of the general tariff, sales and excise structure has been to place at a disadvantage those who use 'gas for cooking and heating. As I understand this item it covers thermostatic devices used in connection with the use of gas, and these will now be brought in under the same rate of duty as thermostatic devices used in connection with the use of coal.

Then it would appear that the answer I got to my other question was wrong, that 443d does not apply to thermostats. Nearly all thermostats used in western Canada in connection with gas heating embody a clock. You set your thermostat at possibly 50 and then it can be set to turn the heat up to 70 at 6, 6.30 or any other time in the morning you want it set for. All those thermostats embody that principle. I understand from what the parliamentary assistant just said that thermostats would not come under 443d.

I wonder if we could have some comment on that. As I said before, those who use natural gas for cooking or heating seem to be discriminated against as far as the tariff, sales tax and excise tax structure are concerned.

Far from it. The change made in item 443d will reduce the duty on gas control devices which are not made in Canada. Because of the greatly increased distribution of natural gas the production of gas-fired apparatus has been greatly extended and the safety measures which must be incorporated in gas-fired apparatus require that these control devices be used. That is why the rate has been reduced. The items

covered by 443e were formerly dutiable as clocks at the rate of 30 per cent plus 40 cents each, and the rate is now brought down to 15 per cent, 22J per cent and 30 per cent.

Why should there be discrimination between devices in connection with the use of gas and the same devices when used in connection with oil? In the west as well as in the east a good deal of oil-burning equipment is being installed for cooking and heating purposes. Gas is piped principally to the large urban centres. Even in the west the smaller rural areas find it difficult to obtain gas, even some towns of considerable population, because it is not considered economically feasible to pipe the gas from the main line. Many farmers living right in gas-producing areas are unable to get gas because it must be piped. But all these people are able to get oil and a great deal is being used today. The same type of thermostat and other apparatus is used. I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant if they have given consideration to these devices on oil-burning furnaces and equipment.

I am also informed that the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Finance have received no representations whatsoever with respect to such apparatus for oil stoves and furnaces. I would only point out that while there may not be such intricate apparatus on oil-burning cooking stoves, there is very intricate apparatus on oil furnaces.

Has the minister made a careful study of what effect the lowering of these tariffs will have on the manufacturers of such goods in the Dominion of Canada? Hon. Douglas Abbott, Minister of Finance, has announced the government's decision to make still another tax reduction. This change brought happy smiles to the faces of farmers.

I should like to ask a question of the Minister cf Finance. In view of the confusion that has developed since the budget speech announcement
Excise Tax Act

That there be imposed, levied and collected an excise tax of fifteen per cent on tires and tubes in

whole or In part of rubber, to be used on trailers or other wheeled attachments used in connection with self-propelled machines.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I believe the best answer I can make to the hon. member for Greenwood is to give him the whole story behind the amendment. This paragraph 4 is designed to extend the 15 per cent tax on replacement tires and tubes so that it will apply to replacement tires and tubes to be used on trailers or other wheeled attachments for use in connection with self-propelled machines.
Prior to the amendment which was made last year to the wording of the provision imposing this tax, the provision read as follows:
(a) Tires in whole or in part of rubber for automotive vehicles of all kinds, including trailers or other wheeled attachments used in connection with any of the said vehicles . . . twenty-five per cent; (b) Inner tubes for use in any such tires . . . twenty-five per cent; Provided that the tax hereby imposed shall not apply to the goods mentioned herein when used exclusively for the original equipment of such automotive vehicles.
The excise tax administration had been ruling that self-propelled machines were "automotive vehicles". However, early in 1952 certain tariff board decisions indicated that self-propelled machines were not automotive vehicles. All this arises from decisions of the tariff board. Accordingly the law was amended last year to regularize the administrative oversight.
By an oversight the amendment was so worded that the tax would apply to the replacement tires and tubes for self-propelled machines but would not be applied to the replacement tires and tubes for self-propelled machine trailers and attachments.
The wording of the amended provision was:
(a) Tires in whole or in part of rubber for self-propelled machines or automotive vehicles of all kinds, including trailers or other wheeled attachments used in connection with any of the said
vehicles	fifteen
per cent; (b) Inner tubes for use in any such tires . . . fifteen per cent; the tax on the articles enumerated in paragraph (a) and (b) of this section does not apply to the goods mentioned therein when used exclusively for the original equipment of such self-propelled machines or automotive vehicles.
The purpose of the resolution now before the committee is therefore to correct the oversight in omitting the words "or self-propelled machines" after the words "the said vehicles"
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1
in the third line. When corrected the law will conform to the intention of the government when the amendment was made last year. As far as replacement tires and tubes for farm implements are concerned, the matter arose out of the worry of certain representatives of the farmers that the effect of the proposed amendment would be to tax something that was not meant to be taxed. What the minister said in the house was that it was not the intention of the government to impose any new tax on farmers. That was not the intention of the resolution and it was not meant that it should be put in the bill. The minister added that tires and tubes when purchased for replacements for farm machinery, including tractors for use on farms for farm purposes, will not be subject to the 15 per cent tax.
I do not have to comment on the article in the Winnipeg Free Press, which I did not read, and with the explanation I have given I think that the matter is crystal clear. There is no difficulty at all. I do not see why the hon. member for Greenwood wants to take the Minister of Finance to task and try to contend that there is some contradiction. There is no contradiction at all. It was never intended to tax farmers or farm machinery by this amendment. He said that consequently farmers could be reassured that tires and tubes when purchased for replacements for farm machinery, including tractors for use on farms for farm purposes, would not be subject to the 15 per cent tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Paragraph 6 of the resolution proposes a change in the application of the sales tax and the 15 per cent excise tax on candy, chocolate, and confectionery in order to remove an anomaly in the present law.
Previously, when a wholesaler or distributor bought these products in bulk quantities from the manufacturer, the 15 per cent tax and the sales tax have been levied on the manufacturer's price for the bulk candy. The wholesaler could then package the merchandise for retail sale.
On the other hand, if the manufacturer had packaged the goods and sold direct to the retailer, the sales tax and the 15 per cent excise tax would be based on a price which would include all the costs of packaging plus the trade mark-up. Therefore, the taxes on candy packaged by the manufacturer would be considerably more than the taxes paid on the same quantity of candy which was packaged by the middleman.
In order to remove this obvious unfairness, the resolution proposes that in these circumstances, instead of requiring the taxes to be paid by the manufacturer, the taxes will be payable by persons, firms or corporations who package these goods for sale, except when the packager is a retailer who packages on his premises for retail sale. That is the case of Laura Secord.

We are indebted to the parliamentary assistant for the explanation he has given, but I would suggest that there is something new involved here with respect to the application of the Excise Tax Act. As I understand, the whole basis of the act hitherto has been the levy of the tax in the first instance on the manufacturer or producer. In previous years some of us have pointed out that the effect of the application of the tax at the manufacturing or producer level has been to bring about a succession of mark-ups on the tax as the goods have passed from the hands of the manufacturer to the wholesaler, then to the jobber, then to the retailer and finally to the consumer. We have been told in reply to these arguments that not only did the present method have simplicity to commend it but administratively it assured that there would be both ease in collecting the tax and no escapes from it. I would point out that while the proposed change, in the circumstances mentioned by the parliamentary assistant, has fairness to commend it, nevertheless we may have to examine the possibility in future of applying

this new method of levying the tax not at the manufacturing or producer level but in the hands of the wholesaler, in other words, the next stage in the process by which goods move from the manufacturer originally into the hands of the consumer eventually.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is not a precedent because we have the same thing in the case of cosmetics. It is section 80, paragraph 5(a), of the Excise Tax Act. Packaging in the candy business and also in the cosmetic business, as these trades now operate, is such an important part of the process of manufacturing the article for delivery to the consumer that really it could be said that the manufacturing process stops at that level.

Mr. Chairman, I also wish to make some general observations about the income tax resolutions. It is just four weeks tonight since we had the budget and there have been four weeks for the taxpayers of Canada to come to know what it amounted to in so far as their interests are concerned. I think they have learned a good deal.
I propose to put on reicord one or two extracts from the press, which has been doing some educating of the taxpayer in the last few weeks. I wish to read first a brief extract from Le Droit of February 23; that was just two days after the budget:
According to our own inquiry, taxpayers in the lower and middle brackets are convinced that the government did not do enough for the Canadian family. This appears to be true as far as we are concerned.
When taxpayers in the lower and middle brackets find out about the small income tax reduction they are getting, they will certainly not be pleased.
I also wish to put on record a quotation from the Calgary Herald of February 26, just a week after the budget. This is entitled "Is it Worth a Package of Smokes?"
Mr. Abbott's election budget is now receiving the "going-over" it deserves at the hands of the opposition critics and all of them appear to be united on at least one point; that the poorest taxpayers are getting the smallest break from smiling Doug.
The majority of Canada's taxpayers earn annually $3,000 or less. Yet a married man with two children who makes $3,000 a year will find that at the end of 1953 his income tax bill has only been reduced by a sum of four dollars or, as one opposition member put it, 33 cents a month. Having cut the cigarette tax at the same time, this will

Income Tax Act
permit the average taxpayer to buy an extra package of cigarettes a month this year, thus increasing the revenue Mr. Abbott will get from the remaining taxes on smokes.
. . . the financial critic of the Progressive-Conservatives had it figured out that the fellow earning just $2,400 a year would receive "the magnificent relief of one dollar a year". We don't think this kind of dollar-a-year man will find much to cheer about in the Liberal budget. . .
As it now stands, the tax cut will be five and one-half per cent for the last six months of the year.
That is the year 1953. That means that the benefit will be received by the taxpayer in 1954.
Who knows what it will be for 1954? Under the "emergencies" of a 1954 budget, Canadians might never see the highly publicized eleven per cent cut in taxes.
I point out that the 11 per cent benefit will not be received until the year 1955.
And in the meantime, the taxpayer will be left in that confused state which benefits governments and elects politicians.
The government has, with this budget, done everything it could have done fust as easily in any one of the past four budgets, while at the same time it has done nothing constructive to economize. It has cut corners but not costs, and by its swift sealing off of any investigation into public administration (such as in defence) it is allowing what Mr. Macdonnell called "waste, extravagance and administrative inefficiency" to flourish at the public's expense.
It is an obvious thing, Mr. Speaker, to see that it is not a budget for the "man in the street", as the newspapers have put it. Our own attitude, as I have indicated, has not been disapproval of what has been done but disapproval of what has not been done. We say that what has been done could have been done and more could have been done too.
We believe that labour has taken this badly. We believe that the small taxpayer whose relief is so microscopic will not take it too well. We feel still more strongly about those who are not income tax payers and who get no benefit from it whatever.
As I say, we claim that other relief which could have been given them has not been given them.
In general, as we say, it has been a budget which has left out of consideration the mass of the people, a matter which they are very speedily waking up to realize.

The rate outs, theoretically, are to be 11 per cent. Actually, because they do not come into effect until July 1, they are 51 per cent.
Take the case of a married man with two children. After this legislation is passed, if he earns $2,400, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Greenwood, he is $1 better off. If he earns $2,500 he is $2 better off. If he earns $2,750, he is $5 better off. If he earns $3,000, he is $7 'better off. These income tax cuts are virtually meaningless to the overwhelming majority of the Canadian people. I have in my hand the latest publication put out by the Department of National Revenue. It is entitled "Taxation Statistics, 1952." It has to do with the year 1950. If any hon. member has that bulletin and wishes to turn to pages 79 and 82, he will find that 92-8 per cent of all taxpayers in Canada who paid income tax earned less than $5,000 for the year under discussion; 2,205,540 citizens paid an average tax of $123. Under this budget that huge number of people-I repeat, 92-8 per cent of all Canadian taxpayers- get an average tax relief of $6.75 each.
I think that the income tax cuts which this government is bringing into effect are little more than an empty gesture. They are of little value to most Canadians. Our citizens were weighed down with heavy income taxes before this budget was introduced, and they are still going to be weighed down by unnecessary and heavy income taxes after this resolution passes.
Government spokesmen like to tell us frequently that Canadian income taxes are the lowest in the world and that Canadian exemptions are the highest. I think the parliamentary assistant made this statement in his budget speech. He was speaking of the income tax in the United Kingdom, the United States and other places. Such a statement may be found at page 2394 of Hansard:
Those figures show that in comparable countries the level of exemptions is much below the level in Canada. I could give example after example of what the status of any taxpayer in any one of these countries would be. They show that any one of them will pay more income tax, more personal income tax, than any individual of comparable status and with the same earnings here in Canada.

I ask you to note those remarks, Mr. Chairman. I challenge the veracity of the statements; and as my authority for challenging their veracity I am going to use Mr. J. Harvey Perry who was, I believe, formerly a taxation expert in the Department of Finance. Mr. Perry is now, of course, working as research director for the Canadian Tax Foundation which is certainly a non-political organization. That particular gentleman published an article in the February issue of the Canadian Tax Journal, and this is what he had to say:
*-Canadian rates of tax are now lower than American . . . but that the privilege of income-splitting allowed to American married taxpayers gives them an advantage over comparable Canadian taxpayers despite the higher American rates.
That article was, of course, written before the current budget resolutions were tabled. I therefore phoned Dr. Eaton in the Department of Finance to get up-to-date Canadian figures for 1953. Those figures are extremely interesting. It is quite true that in some cases the Canadian rates are lower than are the American rates; but in other categories, when you compare Canadian and American tax figures, you find that the American taxes are lower than the Canadian taxes.

That kind of assistance would be something that would help the people who actually need tax relief in this country. If the Canadian people felt that these high income taxes, which the parliamentary assistant is laying before us tonight, were absolutely necessary for the defence effort, I do not think they would object too much; but from the island of Newfoundland right through to British Columbia, a great many people are beginning to wonder whether or not they are getting value for their tax dollar, particularly in defence. There is a general feeling, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Greenwood, that if this government would meet the problem of waste and extravagance-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

-and do something, we might be able to get somewhere.

May I ask the hon. member a question?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

I am not repeating the debate.
Oh, no?

committee of ways and means. The debate on that occasion was not limited to matters in the budget. We cannot go afield, as we did during the debate on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means; but we certainly must be allowed to discuss resolutions that arise from the speech by the Minister of Finance, because that is the essence of the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not objecting to that at all. But I am looking at the resolution which is before the committee right now, and that resolution is concerned with the Income Tax Act. There is one point I would like to answer in what the Minister of Public Works has just said. He said that the debate was concluded last Monday night. My submission is that this is the same debate. It is perfectly proper for any member in the committee of ways and means, under the present resolution, to refer to anything that was said in the budget debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Hon. members know, and I would like them to follow what I shall say- and I shall not be long-that on the motion for the Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means certain amendments are being moved. Now, the discussion normally should be relevant to the amendments that are being moved. But in practice the debate has tended to include all questions pertaining to the government's administration, generally.
Hon. members cannot say that, once they are in committee of ways and means on specific amending resolutions, we can debate all questions which were debated during the budget debate. I am sure that is not what the hon. member means.
No, that is not what I said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand him to mean that whatever was allowable in the general discussion on the original motion that Mr. Speaker leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, having to do with income tax, is now allowable on this Income Tax Act amending resolution-that the same arguments can be advanced? I think that is what he meant.

Let me explain what I meant. I was answering the point made by the minister, that the debate on the motion that Mr. MARCH 19. 1953
Speaker do leave the chair had been concluded on Monday night. The minister said that ended it. My answer is that that is not so. Anything that is related to the resolution is perfectly proper to be brought forward, and the vote on the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair has not closed the debate. Reference can be made now in committee to anything said in the house in that debate, provided it is relevant to the subject matter of the present discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
But it goes further than that. The motion was not only that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair. Her Majesty's loyal opposition moved an amendment which contained four paragraphs; and there was also a subamendment moved concerning definite subjects. The house on three divisions decided on those questions. And once they have been decided by the house I do not think we can revive the debate.
There would be no end to the discussion if we did that. They were specific subjects amending the motion to go into committee. That is our objection.

May I say just another word. I certainly do not contend that you can allow a discussion of everything that was discussed on the motion that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair. For instance, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond made a speech on pipe lines, which was perfectly in order at that time, in that part of the debate, but which certainly would not be in order now.
But I am contending that these resolutions which, in my opinion, are the essence of the budget speech made by the Minister of Finance, are an appropriate subject matter for debate. I do not know how wide a latitude the chairman should allow hon. members in answering statements made at that time. But I think, Mr. Chairman, you should err, if at all, by allowing considerable latitude on the subject, rather than by curtailing it too much.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:

Income Tax Act

Of course I have no alternative, Mr. Chairman, but to bow to your ruling. The tax has been taken out of the man's pay cheque; and as it is generally the company for which the man works that makes up the man's return, the man or woman perhaps does not know that a refund is due. A farmer wrote to me today. He is not only a farmer; he is both a farmer and a fisherman. He told me what his income has been from the land or from the small farm; it is some $1,800. If I were giving him a decision on my own, I would tell him right off that the first thing he should do is to replace his loss and forget about the revenue that came in from fishing or from any other source. But when you come back to the department, what is the department going to say? Are they going to allow that man to take care of the heavy loss he had or are they going to tax him on what they consider to be taxable income? That is what I want to know.

speechtext: It is guaranteed.

speechtext: -those bonds were cashed in the holders would get 100 cents on the dollar-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: It is guaranteed.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: Just a minute-whenever they wanted to sell them. Many of these people are not holding them until maturity. They have to sell them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: They would not be bonds any more.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: But what I wish to do is this; I wish to point out that the minister said this is to avoid double taxation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: To a certain extent.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext:
I am not going into all I said during the budget debate, because I do not think reiteration does any good. But here we have a class of people who, I believe, as my hon. friend from Eglinton said a few moments ago, are being placed in a preferred position. These people may not work, they may not do a tap, and would pay no income tax even if they had incomes of $10,000 a year from stocks.
I am not going into all that, but I do not believe in preferred treatment for any group of citizens. I cannot find any other place to say what I want to say. There are cases in this country of men who are not receiving their incomes from stocks or bonds, but who are receiving it from their own labours.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: You and I.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext:
They are trying to earn their living in spite of handicaps. I want to bring this to the attention of the minister, although I know it is not covered in this particular income tax resolution. The point is this, that we have in this country people who, of necessity, must use automobiles going to and from their work. The expenses of operating those automobiles are not deducted.
Here we have a special concession to wealthy people. I have in mind one or two cases in that category. I have in my hand

a letter from an inspector of income tax who
says:
Unfortunately the income tax law as it stands does not permit the deduction of such an expense from income, and as an administrative body, this division has no alternative but to deny the deduction to all taxpayers including those people who are incapacitated and must rely upon suitable transportation to take them to their place of work.
Yet in respect of corporations, the managements of corporations and stock companies, and executive managers, can use automobiles to drive to and from work. It is part of their business, and part of their deduction. They can charge up the gasoline they use.
I repeat that I know this point is not covered in anything we have before us; but I do say this, that when we are considering deductions again I hope that this matter will be borne in mind. There are very few of these people in this country, and some of them are trying to earn a living under very difficult circumstances.
While many of us are in favour of granting pensions to incapacitated persons, I am not pressing that point now. But an incapacitated person who cannot walk to work should at least be granted the right to a deduction on account of expenditures he may make either for taxicabs or for travelling to and from work in his own motorcar. I suggest that is a plea worthy of consideration. I take this opportunity of making it.
As I say, I do not propose to go into the pros and cons of the matter, because I did so in the budget debate, and I can see no reason for reiterating what I said at that time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: Then, shall we pass on to resolution number 5? Is number 5 carried?

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext:
No; I should like to raise a question concerning this resolution. It provides for deductions in respect of certain provincial taxes as against the dominion tax. The reference is to corporations that are not subject to "certain special provincial taxes". Those are the concluding words in the resolution.
Would the parliamentary assistant enlarge upon what particular provincial taxes are referred to. It will be recalled that it was necessary last year to give some clarification of a similar provision in relation to certain forms of taxes levied in the province of Ontario under the corporation tax act of that province.
In other words there are some special kinds of taxes under that particular provincial statute. Some interpretation was necessary following the signing of the tax agreement last year between the dominion
Income Tax Act
and the government of Ontario. Will the parliamentary assistant enlarge upon the particular provincial taxes referred to here?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext:
In the province of Quebec the following companies are not subject to the 7 per rent corporation income tax: Banks, insurance companies, tramway companies, railway companies, trust companies and mining companies. In lieu of these income taxes they pay some special, specific taxes. For instance, insurance companies pay 2 per cent of premiums received in respect of business transacted in Quebec.
This is a specific tax which is deductible for federal income tax purposes. So that the 7 per cent does not apply.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: I wish to be clear that the deduction under the proposed resolution is going to be extended to corporations in Quebec which pay some of these special kinds of taxes levied on corporations which are not subject to the general corporation levy. Is that what the parliamentary assistant says?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: They are getting them now. The special taxes are deductible. That is why the increase to 7 per cent does not apply to them. They are not paying any provincial corporate income tax in Quebec.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext:
That is not what I am talking about. I am dealing with the corporations which are going to be affected by this proposed change. Are there any special provincial taxes applicable to corporations there, apart from the general corporation levy? I am asking that question in the light of the Ontario experience because as was found last year, in the light of legislation that was brought into question following the agreement entered into between the dominion and the province of Ontario, we had the case of corporations that were liable for taxes under the Ontario corporation tax act, but not for the ordinary flat levy.
There were certain special taxes, for example, on railways operating within the province. I wish to be quite clear that the benefits of this resolution are going to be broad enough to include corporations which are paying any form of provincial corporation taxes now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext:
This applies to the ordinary corporation which pays a corporation income tax. In Quebec, banks, insurance companies and so on pay corporation taxes-in the case of railway companies it is on a mileage basis, and in the case of banks it is on another basis. Those companies are now entitled to a 5 per cent tax credit by virtue of existing legislation. They will not be entitled to the extra 2 per cent under this year's legislation,

Income Tax Act
because they are not paying that corporation tax. But the ordinary commercial corporation will now be entitled to take credit for 7 per cent as against 5 per cent. And other taxes wh'ich have been treated in the past as an expense of doing business will continue to be so treated.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: Are there any other cases than the two mentioned by the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: Those are the only ones I know of in Quebec.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: May I ask the minister about a new 10 per cent tax being levied by the provincial government in British Columbia on logging companies and mining companies? There has been some confusion as to whether or not that tax would be deductible from the dominion income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: I think I answered a question some time ago which was put by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that in the agreements with respect to the rental of corporation taxes entered into with the provinces there is an exception in connection with taxes imposed on mining and logging companies and the provinces continue free to impose taxes on those companies. My understanding is that that is what the present government in British Columbia proposes to do. They are imposing a tax on logging companies. These taxes can be imposed only with respect to logging profits as distinct from milling and manufacturing profits. In the case of the mining companies, they apply only to mining profits as distinct from milling profits.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: Will the amount of that tax be deductible from the dominion corporation tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: No, but it can be deducted as an expense. Half of it will be borne by the taxpayer and roughly half will be at the expense of the federal treasury. It may be deducted as an expense of doing business.

subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: In connection with the effective date, namely January 1, 1953, while I have not given serious thought to it it appears to me that in the case of a corporation whose fiscal year did not coincide with the calendar year it would have to be apportioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: COMPARATIVE TABLE OF INCOME TAX PAID BY WAGE EARNERS CANADA AND U.S.A.
speechtext: Yes.

Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I believe we can dispose of the resolutions concerning the Income Tax Act tomorrow in not too long a time. We would then move to set up the select committee on broadcasting as I believe hon. members are anxious to have that done. We would then take up Bill No. 44, to protect the coastal fisheries; then Bill No. 46, to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act; Bill No. 143, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act; Bill No. 110, to establish the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada; Bill No. 109, to authorize the grant of assistance to a province for the conservation of water resources. Some of these bills are of minor importance and perhaps we could get them through tomorrow.
